notes.meaning: Moses' father-in-law Jethro heard reports of the miracles God worked to rescue Israel from Egypt. Midian lay near the route of travel, so the great news of Pharaoh's defeat quickly reached him. Hearing what the Lord had done stirred Jethro to set out to see Moses in person.

Moses had sent his wife Zipporah and their two boys back to Midian for safety during the dangerous confrontation with Pharaoh in Egypt. The older son's name, Gershom, reminded Moses that he had lived as a foreigner away from his people. The younger son's name, Eliezer, gave thanks to God for being his helper and saving him from Pharaoh's sword.

Jethro brought Moses' family to reunite with him in the wilderness near Mount Sinai, also called the mountain of God. This was the same region where God had first spoken to Moses from the burning bush and promised to bring Israel back to worship Him.
Before entering the camp, Jethro sent a messenger ahead to let Moses know he had arrived with Zipporah and the boys. Sending word in advance was a polite way to prepare Moses for their reunion.

Moses went out to welcome Jethro, bowing down and kissing him according to the respectful customs of the region. Even though Moses had become the leader of a vast nation, he showed humble honor to his father-in-law before bringing him into his tent to talk.

Moses gave Jethro a full report of everything God had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians to set Israel free. He did not hide the struggles they had faced on the journey, but emphasized how the Lord rescued them through each hardship.

Jethro was filled with joy as he listened to how good the Lord had been to Israel. As an outsider to the nation, his gladness stood out in contrast to the frequent grumbling of the Israelites themselves.
Jethro praised the Lord aloud for protecting Moses and delivering the entire nation from slavery. He recognized that Israel's escape from the grip of Pharaoh was entirely the work of God.

Jethro confessed that the Lord is greater than all other gods because He utterly defeated the proud rulers and idols of Egypt. The downfall of the Egyptians proved that human arrogance cannot stand against the true God.

differ.view: Jethro was already a worshipper of the true God through the patriarchal faith of Abraham, and this event simply confirmed what he already believed.
Jethro had previously held a confused faith mixed with the errors of surrounding nations, and he was brought to a genuine and clear knowledge of the true God here.

notes.meaning: Jethro presented offerings to God, and Aaron and the elders of Israel joined him in a sacred meal. Because the formal Levitical priesthood had not yet been established at Sinai, Jethro acted as an honored priest of the true God, and their shared meal sealed their spiritual unity.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Jethro was introducing Moses and Israel to the worship of Yahweh, whom they view as an ancient Kenite or Midianite deity.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: This shared religious meal served as the formal ratification of a treaty of alliance between Israel and the Midianites.

notes.meaning: The morning after the celebration, Moses went right back to his duties as judge, sitting from morning until evening to hear cases. The people lined up all day to have their arguments settled, showing Moses' strong dedication to serving them despite the heavy strain.

Watching the long lines, Jethro asked Moses why he was trying to carry out this judging work completely on his own. Jethro saw that having one man handle every dispute left the people waiting around all day in frustration.

Moses explained that the Israelites came to him to seek God's guidance and receive a fair verdict in their personal disputes. In deciding each case, Moses taught the people God's rules so they would understand how to live righteously.

Jethro warned Moses that his current method was harmful and unsustainable. Trying to hear every single complaint would exhaust Moses physically and test the patience of the entire camp beyond its limits.

Jethro urged Moses to listen to his practical advice, assuring him that God would be with him. Moses' primary calling was to act as the people's go-between before God, bringing their most serious concerns directly to the Lord.

Moses was told to focus his energy on teaching the community God's statutes and laws. By clearly showing the whole nation how they ought to conduct themselves and what duties were expected of them, Moses could prevent many disputes before they even started.

Jethro advised Moses to pick out capable, honest men who feared God and could not be bribed with money. These trusted men would then be placed over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens to maintain order.

These newly appointed leaders were to handle ordinary disagreements at all times, freeing Moses from minor issues. Only the most difficult cases would be passed upward to Moses, sharing the workload so that his burden became much lighter.

Jethro reminded Moses to check this counsel with God to ensure the Lord commanded it. If God approved the plan, Moses would have the stamina to keep leading, and the people could get their cases settled quickly and go home content.

Moses showed true humility by taking the advice of his father-in-law instead of assuming he knew best. He recognized the practical wisdom in Jethro's words and prepared to put the entire plan into action.

Moses selected qualified, trustworthy leaders from among all the tribes and placed them over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. These men faithfully handled the everyday legal matters of the camp, while referring only the hardest questions to Moses.

After the new leaders were settled in their roles, Moses gave Jethro a warm farewell, and Jethro journeyed back to Midian. He returned home having strengthened Moses' household and helped establish a peaceful system of justice for Israel.
